children: A key gauge of leveraged speculation has cooled from extreme territory, even as U.S. stocks remain near record highs.

Wellington-Altus highlighted that the 15-month rate of change in FINRA customer debit balances — the amount investors have borrowed against securities in margin accounts — has slipped back below 60%. That series is widely treated as a proxy for how aggressively traders are using borrowed money to chase equities.

The latest official print shows debit balances at $1.45 trillion in August 2026, up from July but below June’s $1.50 trillion peak and still roughly 40% higher than a year earlier. The raw dollar total tends to rise with prices; the 15-month pace of change is what analysts watch for excess.

Similar spikes above that 60% threshold appeared ahead of the 2000, 2007, and late-2021 market peaks. In each case, the subsequent rollover in the rate of change coincided with major tops on the S&P 500 (
). The current monthly chart of the index sits near those prior inflection points after a multi-year advance.

The reading is not a timing trigger by itself. Margin debt can stay elevated for months, and brokerage borrowing excludes bank securities-backed loans, futures leverage and options. Still, a retreat from the “greed” zone after such a rapid buildup is the same pattern that has marked the later stages of prior bull markets. Investors will watch the next FINRA release, due in the third week of October, to see whether the deceleration continues.

title: FINRA leverage pace cools — Same signal seen at 2000, 2007, 2021 tops
